To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the metabolic transformation of pyrethoids in insect tissues involves the formation of a number of metabolites that are not produced in vertebrates, and that these metabolites have different toxicities than the parent compounds.

(1) the metabolic fate of the trans and cis isomer of a given pyrethroid is similar in all tissues studied (fat body, Malpighian tubules, and brain), (2) the metabolic pathways are similar in all species tested (Drosophila, Musca, and Blattella), and (3) the rate of metabolism of the cis isomer is greater than that of the trans isomer.

the cis isomers of the pyrethroids are more toxic than the trans isomers because the cis isomers are more stable than the trans isomer in insect tissues and therefore more readily accumulate at the site of action.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of metabolism on the structure-activity relationships observed for pyrethroids, and with the effects of the structure of the insecticide on the metabolism of these compounds in insects.
the elucidation of the molecular basis of the insecticidal properties of synthetic pyrethroids.
the development of novel pyrethroid structures with improved selectivity for insects over mammals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the observed differences in toxicity between cis and trans isomers of pyretinoids are due to differences in the pharmacokinetics of these compounds, with the trans isomers being more readily metabolized and eliminated than the cis isomers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
non-neural factors contribute significantly to the differences in toxicity observed between trans and cis pyrethroids and between the two cis isomers.
non-neural factors can be of major importance and that the effects of these factors are often not predictable.

, while non-neural processes can influence pyrethroid potency and selectivity, they are not sufficient to account for the large differences in potency between the trans and cis isomeric forms of pyrethoids.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the differences in insect toxicity between the cis and trans isomers of pyrrethroids arise primarily from differences in the rates of metabolism of these isomers in the insect.
the differences in insecticidal activity between trans and cis isomeric pairs are due primarily to differences in their pharmacokinetics.
, in general, the pharmacokinetic differences between the trans and cis isomer of a given pyrethroid are greater than the toxicological differences.
